entities.name: PMID:25081898
observations: Dutch probabilistic economic model compared tumor testing for colorectal cancer diagnosed at ≤70 versus ≤50 years, including cascade testing of relatives.
The ≤70 strategy detected approximately fourfold more Lynch syndrome patients; number needed to test increased from 19 to 42 and testing cost per carrier from €4,837 to €9,437.
Including cascade screening, incremental cost was €2,703 per additional life-year gained; authors judged testing CRC tumors diagnosed at ≤70 years highly cost-effective.

entities.name: PMID:29300371
observations: Systematic review found two economic evaluations supporting age-targeted colorectal cancer Lynch syndrome screening with a cutoff of 70 years versus lower thresholds.
The review concluded that universal or ≤70-year age-targeted CRC-based screening is cost-effective, while noting heterogeneity and uncertainty across models.

entities.name: PMID:31595523
observations: Australian lifetime microsimulation evaluated tumor testing at all ages and age limits under 50, 60, and 70 years in patients with colorectal cancer and relatives.

Universal tumor-testing strategies had ICERs of approximately A$28,915–31,904 per life-year saved versus no testing; immunohistochemistry plus BRAF testing with two-yearly surveillance had ICERs of A$11,525–32,153 per life-year saved across age limits.

entities.name: Lynch syndrome
observations: Hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome for which tumor mismatch-repair testing can identify patients requiring confirmatory germline testing and cascade testing of relatives.

entities.name: Age 50 to 70 testing
observations: Raising the colorectal cancer tumor-testing eligibility threshold from age 50 to 70 is modeled as cost-effective when cascade testing and preventive surveillance are included.
The conclusion depends on testing costs, number of relatives tested, surveillance adherence, and local willingness-to-pay thresholds; evidence is model-based rather than randomized.
